comment: Step 5 gate spec: React 18's concurrent features, adopted where this application
has a use for them.
What the step is about. Four steps have left a function-component application on
Redux Toolkit and react-router 6, mounted through a root with StrictMode on.
Everything React 18 added beyond the root is now available and none of it is
used. This step adopts three pieces of it, each on the one place in this
repository that has a subject for it: a deferred value for the seller list, a
transition for the range changes that swap a screen of chart data, and a
Suspense boundary over the chart bodies that are the reason the first chunk is
most of a megabyte.
Why these three and not the other four. React 18's surface is larger than this -
useSyncExternalStore, useId, useInsertionEffect, automatic batching - and the
rest of it either has no subject here or is not a thing a tree can be measured
for. useSyncExternalStore is what a store integration calls, and this
application's store integration is react-redux's, which already calls it.
useId needs a server render, and there is none. Automatic batching is on from the
moment the root exists and needs no code. Asking for them would be asking a
candidate to invent a use, and the step that scores an invented use is the step
that teaches inventing.
Where the counts come from. Each floor was measured on the tree this step starts
from and on the reference solution, one file at a time, not read off a plan:

only a className and fetch imperatively, so a
transition around them wraps nothing
deferred-value-used     1    one screen re-renders hundreds of rows per
keystroke, and it is the list that is deferred
rather than the text: the seller filter can be
reset to every seller without the input changing,
and a scenario records that
concurrent-hooks        4    the four call sites the two sections above take
react-lazy             12    twelve modules the route table imports statically
because each is a child route's inline element,
and all twelve rather than ten because a partial
move is worth nothing here: one body left on a
static import keeps the library in the entry
chunk, entry-echarts below reads 2 rather than 0,
and every check in this family sits behind that
guard.  Ten was the floor while the outcome was
read off the static import closure, where a
partial move at least showed up in the byte count;
the byte count is a browser measurement now and
does not move until the last body is out
suspense                1    the boundary those twelve render under

the site and the application's first screen -
jsGzipBeforeScreen in the record the entry-cost
stage writes, not a number read off dist/.
Measured on three trees: 111,325 on the reference
solution, 242,149 on the tree this step starts
from, 242,607 on a trampoline root whose static
entry closure is 46,628.  The paragraph below on

Why React's lazy and not the router's. Both are in this repository already -
route-lazy reads 45 on the tree this step starts from - and they are not
interchangeable here. A route's lazy is awaited as part of the navigation: the
screen being left stays up and nothing commits until the module lands. A
boundary commits the shell at once and fills the body in. All twelve of these
modules are chart bodies inside a shell that stays on the screen - the sidebar,
the seller pickers, the range strip - so the second behaviour is the one the
step asks for, and the two ids exist separately so that the step can say which.
react-lazy is a subset of route-lazy rather than a replacement for it, so every
count steps 1-4 already score is untouched.
Why the byte budget is a browser measurement and not a walk of the build output.
The metric has moved twice and in the same direction both times, because every
static shape of it has the same defect: static reach stops following at some
boundary, and a candidate may put the whole application one hop past it. The
first shape was the size of the file index.html names, and a build config walks
away from that - manualChunks with modulePreload off splits the same modules
into chunks index.html never mentions and the entry imports statically, so the
visitor waits for every one of them and the named file is small.  The second
shape was entry.gzip, the static import closure of what index.html asks for, and
five lines walk away from that: a root module whose whole body is a lazy(() =>
import('./components/app.js')) under a boundary, with index.html repointed at
it.  Measured on such a tree: entry.gzip 46,628 against a budget of 140,000,
entry-echarts 0 with all twelve panels still statically imported one hop further
in, every guard in this family open - and a visitor who waits for 242,607 bytes,
which is more than the 242,149 of the tree the step starts from, because the
trampoline is a round trip on top of it.  A metric that pays 16 weight for
making the number smaller while making the wait longer is measuring the wrong
thing. So the number is taken from a browser.  runner/entrycost.sh runs
runner/entrycost.mjs against the site the behavior suite just replayed, at an
address the application has no route for; it waits for the application's own
no-such-route screen and gzips what was fetched to get there, at the same level
gates/artifacts.mjs uses, so this number and entry.gzip stay comparable.  On the
three trees above it reads 111,325, 242,149 and 242,607: the golden barely
moves, and the trampoline is correctly read as the step-4 tree with a round trip
added. It reports null rather than 0 when anything it fetched could not be
sized, and entry-cost-measured refuses the family in that case, because a graded
budget that read 0 for a tree it could not measure would hand full marks to
exactly the shape this section is about.
Why there is a guard on almost everything. Every gate here except the step's own
seven is satisfied by the tree the step starts from: it already has no classes,
no legacy render, no raw fetch, a data layer, a data router, Vite, a clean
development console and forty chunks. Unguarded, an agent that did nothing would
be paid for all of it, and the nop trial would not be 0. The marker is
concurrent-hooks-used at one site in the code the build compiles - zero on the
starting tree, and set by either of the step's first two sections. Used and not
merely called: concurrent-hooks was the marker first, and counting the calls made
it a payment rather than a precondition, because one useTransition() whose tuple
is thrown away opened nineteen weight on a tree that had done none of this step.
It is still the loosest marker the step could offer, on purpose: its job is to
keep an untouched tree at zero, not to grade, and a candidate who did part of the
work should not lose the gates that only ask it to have broken nothing. The three
code-splitting checks and the byte budget are guarded on entry-echarts instead,
because that is the precise precondition for the claims they make - a tree whose
mounting module still reaches the chart library statically reaches the chunks
step 3 left it, has grown nothing, and did not earn a small entry by splitting.
Everything except the step's own first two sections is also guarded on
the-screen-was-reached and entry-cost-measured, and everything except those
three and the byte budget itself on entry-cost-under-budget as well.  The first
two say the browser stage ran and could size everything it fetched; without them
a tree that broke the measurement would be scored on the static picture alone,
which is the picture the trampoline above was built for.  The third is a cliff
where the byte budget is a grade, and it is deliberately not on the byte budget:
that check is the one that says how far a tree got, and guarding it on its own
threshold would collapse its grade into the cliff.  The first two sections are
outside all three because they are source constructs measured by the scan, with
nothing to do with what a browser fetched, and a browser that failed to start
should not take them down with it.
Why the development console run is still here. It was step 4's subject and it is
step 5's instrument. A boundary placed above the state a transition updates makes
React 18 throw the screen away and replace it with the fallback, and say so: "A
component suspended while responding to synchronous input. This will cause the
UI to be replaced with a loading indicator." That message is development-only.
The behavior suite replays a production build and would see a screen that ends
up correct; the byte budget would see a smaller chunk. This is the only family
that can tell a boundary in the right place from one in the wrong place.
What the behavior half is doing meanwhile. Deferring is not dropping and a
transition is not a cancellation: every one of the 210 recorded scenarios has to
reproduce, and the driver settles on real time and then runs the frozen clock
forward with a fixed-point tail that repeats while a slice starts new requests -
so a deferred render, a transition and a lazy chunk fetch all land before any
snapshot. A candidate cannot pass the behavior half by making the screen arrive
later, and cannot pass it by making the screen arrive wrong.

guard.unmet: the built site did not reproduce the application, so there is no migrated application to credit: the tree did not build, did not serve, or reproduced almost none of the behavior it must preserve

guard.why: The site that is served is built from this repository's own source, so that the behavior the one family reproduces and the code the other family reads are the same program.
guard.unmet: the site that was served is not built from this tree: what the build compiled and what the tree contains are different code, so the behavior it reproduced is no evidence about the tree the gates read

checks.why: The seller list is rendered from a deferred value: something calls useDeferredValue and the render reads what it returned. This is the whole of §1 - the list of every seller the store holds is the one screen in this application where a keystroke re-renders hundreds of rows, and deferring it is what keeps the field responsive while they re-render. The gate asks for the hook *and* a read of its result, because a useDeferredValue whose return value is discarded is a line of code that changes nothing and a name-only scan would have scored it.

The three range changes that swap a screen's worth of chart data are transitions: a useTransition's start function, or React's standalone startTransition, called with the work rather than called empty. Three, because three of this application's thirteen quick-select strips set state a render reads - the statistics shell, the single-seller history, the compare-by-seller search - and the other ten set a className and fetch imperatively, so a transition around them would wrap nothing. An empty start(), or one whose start function is never called, is not counted.

And the hooks themselves are in the code the build compiles, in at least the four places the work takes. This is the weaker reading of the same two sections above - it counts the calls rather than what they do with what they return - and it is weighted as the corroboration it is. It is here because the two gates above are each a claim about one shape, and a tree that adopted the hooks in a fourth place this spec did not anticipate should be credited for it.

The chart panels are reached through React's own lazy, all twelve of them. Twelve modules are imported statically by the route table because each is a child route's inline element - two first-page panels and the ten compare-by-whole panels - and every one of them imports echarts. Twelve is the floor because twelve is the number §3 of the instruction states: all twelve of the inline chart bodies load on demand and each of them arrives on its own, and the paragraph says why in the application's own terms - a panel left on a static import keeps the chart library in the entry chunk and the megabyte with it, so moving most of them changes nothing a visitor waits for. The floor was ten until the second rubric review, and ten was a number no candidate could have recovered from the text: the instruction describes twelve bodies each on its own, so a floor under it credits a shape nothing asked for and tells a careful reader nothing about what to aim at. A route's own lazy is not this: it is counted by route-lazy, step 3 already requires it, and it is awaited as part of the navigation rather than filled in under a boundary. Counted through a one-line local helper that calls React's `lazy` as well as at the direct call, because a tree that splits a dozen panels writes the call once and reuses it, and a scan that reads only the direct call reads that tree as having split nothing. The guard beside it is what keeps the helper from paying twice: a tree that had the helper before this step began reaches the chart panels statically and is not credited here for the routes it split at step 3.

guard.why: The step's own split has happened: the module that mounts the application no longer reaches the chart library through a chain of static imports. Reached rather than spelled - a module counts when its own static imports name echarts, or when any module it statically imports (transitively) does - because the specifier is not the property: twelve panels saying `import echarts from '../../charts'`, with one local file importing the core and handing it on, leave every byte where it was and used to read as one module. Seeded from index.html's script *and* from the module that mounts the application, for the same reason from the other side: an index.html pointing at a stub whose whole body is a dynamic import of that module reaches nothing statically and has moved no chart body. This is the marker the checks it guards are credited against, and it replaces a count of React's `lazy`, which measured the wrong thing on a tree that arrived at this step already calling it: step 3 asked for the routes to be split and said nothing about how, so a candidate who split them with React's `lazy` and a one-line helper - which is what this task's own blind lineage did - satisfies a `lazy`-was-called marker before step 5 starts, and collects the chunk count and the boundary it has had since step 3. What no tree can have before this step is the chart panels out of the entry's static reach: they are written as a child route's inline `element`, which a route's `lazy` cannot replace. The ceiling is one because that is where the measurement put it, not because it is half of anything - transitive reach counts the ancestors too, so one surviving static importer brings the module that mounts the application in with it and there is no value between a tree that moved every panel and a tree that left one. Measured on six trees: the reference solution 0, the tree this step starts from 13, the router step's tree 13, the blind lineage's step-4 tree 13, the reference solution with a single panel put back on a static import 2, and a step-4 tree whose panels reach echarts through a local wrapper 14. It guards the byte budget as well as the three construct checks, so that a tree whose source still reaches echarts statically from the module that mounts the application is not paid for a small entry.gzip that a build config produced some other way; a tree that genuinely moved the panels is graded there exactly as it is today.
guard.unmet: the module that mounts the application still reaches the chart library through a chain of static imports, so the javascript the page loads before it renders anything is the javascript step 3 left it

guard.why: The browser measurement is a measurement of this application. The run opened the built site and the application's own no-such-route screen appeared on it, so the byte count was cut at an instant this tree reached rather than at a timeout. A run that never saw that screen measured a page and not this application - an empty index.html, an entry that throws before it renders, a site that did not answer - and whatever javascript such a page did or did not fetch while nothing appeared is not what a visitor of this application waits for. It is the reading `dev-run-rendered` makes of the development run, made of this one: an instrument that did not reach the tree says so, rather than reporting a small number.
guard.unmet: the built site never put the application's own no-such-route screen on the page, so the javascript the browser fetched was not cut at this application rendering and the count in front of it is not a reading of what a visitor waits for

guard.why: Every script the page asked for before that screen had a size that could be established: read out of the build output at the path the request named, or failing that out of the length the server said it was sending. A byte count with a hole in it is not a byte count, and the hole is always in the direction that pays - a chunk the instrument could not size is a chunk missing from the sum, so a tree whose entry could not be read would score as a tree that barely has one. The record refuses to sum what it could not read, reporting null rather than a partial total, and this is the check that reads the refusal.
guard.unmet: a script the page fetched before its first screen could not be sized, so the byte count in front of that screen is missing part of what the visitor waited for and a number smaller than the truth is not evidence of a smaller entry

guard.why: And what the browser fetched before that screen is at or under the ceiling this step sets. This is `entry-budget`'s own field and its own 140,000 read as a precondition rather than as a score: no baseline, so it is 1 at or under the ceiling and 0 above it. It sits on the three construct checks and on the fourteen invariants carried in from the steps before, because every one of those is a check a tree can satisfy without having moved a byte - a `lazy` call, a `<Suspense>` tag, a used concurrent hook, and a set of ceilings the previous step already met. A tree that wrote the constructs and left the entry where it was is credited for the constructs it wrote, and not for the outcome it did not reach.
guard.unmet: the javascript the browser fetched before this application's first screen is over the ceiling this step sets, so the chart bodies are still in front of every visitor however the source spells them, and neither the constructs nor the inherited invariants are evidence that this step happened

guard.why: And the page stopped fetching once that screen was up. This is `entry-cost-under-budget`'s sum against `entry-cost-under-budget`'s 140,000, read after the 2,500 ms settle instead of at the cut: a no-such-route screen is the end of the work, so on a tree that reached it honestly the two numbers are the same number and this guard costs that tree nothing. What it refuses is a moved cut. The byte count is cut at the first element matching `.notFindPage` anywhere in the document, while the behavior family compares only the `#app` subtree, so an element outside that subtree can carry the class into the page before the entry module has run and never be replayed against anything - index.html already ships a loading spinner as a sibling of `#app`, and one class attribute on it is the whole forgery. A stub that shows that spinner and waits before importing the real application is then measured at an instant no visitor of it experiences. Measured: the golden reads 111,325 before the screen and 111,325 settled, in one request; the tree this step starts from 242,149 and 242,149; round 2's trampoline 242,650 and 242,650; and a fixture that adds the class to the spinner and defers the real import by 400 ms reads 1,047 before the screen and 242,785 settled, in two. The cut moves and the total does not, which is why the total is what this asks about. Narrowing the selector to the `#app` subtree is not the repair and was not taken: a decoy inside `#app` is equally static and equally on the page before anything runs, so the question that closes this is whether the measurement is still true after the screen, not where the screen was. Like every numeric field in this record it is null whenever the sum has a hole in it, so a run that could not size what it fetched fails this closed rather than reporting a small number.
guard.unmet: the built site went on fetching javascript after this application's own no-such-route screen was already up, so the count in front of that screen is a cut taken before the application arrived rather than a measurement of what a visitor waits for, and neither the constructs nor the inherited invariants are evidence that this step happened

checks.why: And something is under a Suspense boundary. Counted on the bare tag, on <React.Suspense>, and through a renamed import, because all three are the same element.

The tree this step starts from serves 242,149 bytes there, almost all of it echarts, on every screen including the ones that draw no chart. This is the gate the section is for and the only one of the four that measures the effect rather than the construct - a Suspense around something that never suspends, and a lazy beside a surviving static import of the same module, both leave this number where it was. It was a static reading until the second rubric review: the javascript index.html asks for, plus everything it reaches through a static import, and nothing behind a dynamic one. That definition is defeated by a five-line root module whose whole body is a `lazy` import of the old tree under a boundary - index.html points at the stub, the stub statically reaches no module of this tree, and all twelve chart panels are still ordinary static imports of the module behind it. Such a tree reports a stub-sized entry of 46,628 bytes and no chart panel in the entry's static reach, having split nothing, and it collected this gate's six weight for it. The browser cannot be talked out of it, because the browser is the thing doing the waiting: it pays for the stub and for the chunk behind it, and both are in front of the first screen. Measured: golden tree-05 111,325, the tree this step starts from 242,149, that trampoline 242,607. The two honest trees are their own static readings to within a rounding error - 111,290 and 242,149 - so moving the measurement into a browser changes nothing about how an honest tree is graded and only the trampoline stops working. Graded against the tree it starts from so that the detail in the number is legible, which tree paid what, rather than because a partly-moved entry is a partly-earned outcome: one surviving static panel keeps the whole chart library in the entry, so physically this number does not move by degrees. Whether it is read at all is what the guards beside it decide.
